content.statement: A target such as "the API answers 99 % of requests within 200 ms" is a non-functional requirement.

remember: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional ones set measurable targets such as latency, availability and cost.

content.prompt: A product owner says the new search "must be fast". What is the most useful thing to ask next?

options.text: Which database should the search use?
Which programming language is fastest for search?
How fast, and for what share of requests? For example, 95 % within 300 ms
Should we put a cache in front of the search?

remember: Turn vague wishes like "fast" into numbers (95 % within 300 ms) before choosing any technology.

content.prompt: Three of these are non-functional requirements. Which one is a functional requirement?

items.text: Users can reset their password by email
Search results appear within 1 second for 95 % of queries
The service is available 99.9 % of each month
No confirmed order is lost if one server dies

remember: A functional requirement is something the user can do; non-functional ones describe how well the system must do it.

content.prompt: Match each requirement with the quality it describes.

left.text: A confirmed payment is never lost
Handles ten times the usual traffic by adding servers

right.text: Durability
Scalability
Latency
Availability

remember: Latency is speed, availability is uptime, durability is not losing data, and scalability is growing with load.

content.prompt: Put the usual steps of designing a new system in order.

steps.text: Draw the high-level design
Estimate traffic and storage
Deep-dive into the bottlenecks
Clarify functional and non-functional requirements

remember: Requirements first, then rough numbers, then the big picture, then the details where the numbers say it will hurt.

content.statement: For a peak-traffic estimate, you can assume a day's requests are spread evenly over all 24 hours.

remember: Traffic is uneven over the day; size the system for the peak, often a few times the daily average.

content.prompt: 1 million daily users each make 20 requests a day, and the peak hour has 3 times the average rate. About how many requests per second must the system handle at peak?

options.text: About 230
About 2,300
About 40,000
About 700

remember: 1 million requests a day is about 12 per second; multiply by the peak factor before sizing servers.

content.prompt: A quick traffic estimate. What does this print?

remember: A day has 86,400 seconds, so 10 million requests a day is only about 115 per second on average.

content.prompt: The estimate prints 7,300,000 TB of photos over 5 years, far more than a sanity check gives. Find the bug.
content.code:
photos_per_day = 2_000_000
avg_photo_mb = 2
days = 5 * 365

total_mb = photos_per_day * avg_photo_mb * days
total_tb = total_mb / 1000
print(f"{total_tb:,.0f} TB over 5 years")

fixes.text: Divide total_mb by 1024 instead of 1000
Divide total_mb by 1,000,000
Divide total_mb by 8 to turn bits into bytes

remember: 1 TB is a million MB; check the units at every step, because an estimate a thousand times off is usually one wrong conversion.

content.prompt: Order these operations from fastest to slowest.

steps.text: Random read from an SSD
Network round trip between Europe and the US
Read a value from main memory (RAM)
Disk seek on a spinning hard drive
Read from the CPU's L1 cache

remember: Rough orders of magnitude: L1 cache 1 ns, RAM 100 ns, SSD read 100 µs, disk seek 10 ms, an intercontinental round trip 100 ms or more.

content.statement: A stateless service can handle a user's next request on any of its instances.

remember: When no instance keeps client state between requests, the load balancer may send each request anywhere.

content.prompt: What makes a web service stateless?

options.text: It keeps no client data in its own memory between requests
It never writes anything to a database
It does not use cookies or tokens
It restarts after every request it serves

remember: Stateless means no client data stays in the instance between requests; state lives in the request, a token or a shared store.

content.prompt: The app runs on 3 instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Login succeeds, but /me then often answers 401. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Give the cookie a maxAge so it lasts longer
Keep sessions in a shared store such as Redis
Make the /me handler async and await sessions.get

remember: Session state in one instance's memory is invisible to the others; keep it in a shared store or a signed token.

content.prompt: The API runs on 3 instances that are replaced on every deploy. Uploaded avatars must be kept for good and be readable from every instance. Fill the blank.

options.text: localDisk.write
processMemory.set
cacheWithOneHourTtl.set
objectStorage.put

remember: Files on an instance's disk vanish with it and are invisible to the other instances; put uploads in shared object storage.

content.prompt: Three of these stop you from adding instances freely behind a load balancer. Which one does not?

items.text: Per-user rate-limit counters kept in each instance's memory
Settings read from environment variables at startup
Shopping carts kept in a global variable
Background jobs queued in an array in process memory

remember: Read-only config is the same on every instance; anything a request changes must live outside the process.

content.statement: A load balancer keeps sending requests to a server that fails its health checks until someone removes it by hand.

remember: Health checks let a load balancer take a failing server out of rotation on its own and add it back when it recovers.

content.prompt: Why put a load balancer in front of three identical app servers?

options.text: To cache database query results for the servers
To spread requests over them and skip any server that is down
To keep the code on the three servers in sync
To let the three servers share one block of memory

remember: A load balancer spreads traffic over servers and routes around the ones that fail.

content.prompt: Match each load-balancing algorithm with how it picks a server.

right.text: Sends the same client address to the same server
Takes turns, but bigger servers get more turns
Takes turns: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3
Picks the server with the fewest open connections

remember: Round robin takes turns, weights favour bigger servers, least connections follows current load, and hashing keeps a client on one server.

content.prompt: A round-robin balancer skips unhealthy servers. What does this print?

remember: Round robin cycles over the healthy servers only: an unhealthy server's turn passes to the next healthy one.

content.prompt: You deploy a new version to server b, one of three behind a load balancer, without failing a single request. Put the steps in order.

steps.text: Wait until b passes its health checks
Take b out of the pool so it gets no new requests
Put b back into the pool
Let b finish the requests it is already handling
Install and start the new version on b

remember: Drain before you stop: remove the server, let in-flight requests finish, upgrade, wait until it is healthy, then add it back.

content.statement: A cache helps most with data that changes on every request and is rarely read twice.

remember: Caching pays off for data that is read often and changes rarely.

content.prompt: Which description matches write-through caching?

options.text: Each write deletes the cache entry, and the next read reloads it
Each write goes to the cache first and reaches the database later
Each write skips the cache, and old entries expire by TTL
Each write updates the cache and the database in the same operation

remember: Write-through writes the cache and the database together; write-back delays the database write; cache-aside deletes and reloads on the next read.

content.prompt: A cache-aside read. Fill the blank.
content.code:
def get_user(user_id):
    key = f"user:{user_id}"
    user = cache.get(key)
    if user is None:
        user = db.load_user(user_id)
        ____
    return user

options.text: cache.delete(key)
cache.set(key, user, ttl=300)
db.save_user(user)
return cache.get(key)

remember: In cache-aside the application reads the cache, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result with a TTL.

content.prompt: The price changes in the database, but nothing invalidates the cache. What does this print?
content.code:
TTL = 60
db = {"price": 10}
cache = {}  # key -> (value, expires_at)

def read(key, now):
    hit = cache.get(key)
    if hit and now < hit[1]:
        return hit[0]
    cache[key] = (db[key], now + TTL)
    return db[key]

a = read("price", now=0)
db["price"] = 12
b = read("price", now=30)
c = read("price", now=61)
print(a, b, c)

remember: Without invalidation a cached value can stay stale for up to the full TTL after the database changes.

content.prompt: After a user changes their email, the profile keeps showing the old one for about 10 more minutes. Find the bug.
content.code:
TTL = 600

def get_user(user_id):
    key = f"user:{user_id}"
    user = cache.get(key)
    if user is None:
        user = db.fetch_user(user_id)
        cache.set(key, user, ttl=TTL)
    return user

def update_email(user_id, email):
    db.update_user(user_id, email=email)
    # refresh the cached copy
    cache.set(f"user:{user_id}", get_user(user_id),
              ttl=TTL)

fixes.text: Lower TTL to 60 so stale entries expire sooner
Move the cache.set call above db.update_user
Replace it with cache.delete(f"user:{user_id}")

remember: On a write, delete the cache key or fill it from the database; refreshing through the cached read path just saves the stale copy again.

content.statement: A CDN keeps copies of static files on servers near users, so fewer requests reach the origin server.

remember: A CDN answers from edge servers close to users and only goes to the origin on a miss.

content.prompt: The site's images are served from one server in Germany. Users in Australia say they load slowly. What helps them most?

options.text: Give the German server more CPU and RAM
Add a second server next to the first one in Germany
Serve the images through a CDN
Add an index to the images table

remember: Distance adds latency that more CPU cannot remove; a CDN serves static files from near the user.

content.prompt: Match each CDN term with its meaning.

right.text: A CDN server near users that keeps copies
Removing a file from every edge cache before its TTL ends
Share of requests answered without asking the origin
The server that holds the original content

remember: The origin holds the content, edges keep copies near users, the hit ratio says how often edges suffice, and a purge removes copies early.

content.prompt: A CDN caches responses and serves each cached copy to every visitor. Three of these are safe to cache that way. Which one is not?

items.text: GET /api/cart, which finds the user through a session cookie
GET /assets/app.3f9a1c.js, named by its content hash
GET /images/logo.png
GET /api/products?page=2, the same for every visitor

remember: Only share cached copies of responses that are identical for every visitor; per-user responses must be private or not cached.

content.prompt: Hashed bundles are cached for a year. After a deploy, users must get the new index.html at once, yet an unchanged index.html should not be downloaded again. Fill the header.
content.code:
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
ETag: "v42"
Cache-Control: ____

options.text: no-cache
max-age=31536000, immutable
no-store
max-age=86400

remember: no-cache still stores a copy but checks with the server before each use (a cheap 304 if unchanged); no-store never keeps one.

content.statement: Right after a write to the primary, a read replica may still return the old value.

remember: Replicas apply changes a little later than the primary, so a read right after a write can be stale.

content.prompt: Which workload gains the most from adding read replicas?

options.text: An event log that inserts 20,000 rows per second and is rarely read
A product catalog that is read about 1,000 times for every write
A counter that every request increments
A database whose disk is almost full

remember: Every replica copies every write and only shares the reads, so replicas help read-heavy workloads, not write-heavy ones or full disks.

content.prompt: The replica applies each write 2 seconds after the primary. What does this print?
content.code:
LAG = 2
log = []  # (time, key, value) written on the primary

def write(t, key, value):
    log.append((t, key, value))

def read_replica(t, key):
    value = None
    for wt, k, v in log:
        if k == key and wt + LAG <= t:
            value = v
    return value

write(0, "bio", "old")
write(10, "bio", "new")
print(read_replica(1, "bio"), read_replica(11, "bio"),
      read_replica(12, "bio"))

options.text: old new new
None old new
old old new
None new new

remember: With replication lag a replica shows what the primary had a moment ago, which can even be "not there yet".

content.prompt: Users save a new bio and the confirmation page often shows the old one; a refresh a moment later shows the new bio. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Read the profile from the primary right after the write
Run the UPDATE inside an explicit transaction
Add an index on users.id on the replica

remember: Read your own writes: right after a user changes data, read it from the primary, not from a replica that may lag.

content.prompt: Replicas lag a few seconds behind the primary. Three of these reads can safely go to a replica. Which one should go to the primary?

items.text: Last month's sales report
A public product page
Search results for "red shoes"
The account balance checked right before approving a withdrawal

remember: Send reads that must see the latest write, like a balance before a withdrawal, to the primary; the rest can tolerate lag.

content.statement: In a sharded database, every shard holds a full copy of all the data.

remember: Shards split the data so each holds only its part; full copies are replicas.

content.prompt: An orders table is sharded by customer_id. Which query is the most expensive?

options.text: All orders of customer 42
Order 9001 of customer 42, with both ids known
The 10 newest orders of customer 42
Total revenue per product across all orders

remember: A query that includes the shard key hits one shard; a query across all keys must ask every shard and merge the results.

content.prompt: Users are placed on shards with user_id % n. The cluster grows from 3 to 4 shards. What does this print?
content.code:
def shard(user_id, n):
    return user_id % n

users = range(12)
moved = [u for u in users if shard(u, 3) != shard(u, 4)]
print(len(moved), moved[:3])

remember: With hash mod N, changing N moves most keys; consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of them.

content.prompt: Events are spread over 8 databases, yet all of today's inserts go to one database at 100 % CPU while the other 7 sit idle. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Raise SHARDS to 32
Hash event["user_id"] instead of the day
Use SHA-256 of the day instead of stable_hash

remember: A shard key that all current writes share, like today's date, makes a hot shard; pick a key with many values in use at once.

content.prompt: Match each way of assigning rows to shards with its trade-off.

left.text: Lookup table from tenant to shard

right.text: Any tenant can be moved alone, but every query first needs the mapping
Date-range queries hit one shard, but all new rows land on the newest
Even spread, and adding a shard moves only a small share of rows
Even spread, but changing N moves most rows

remember: Ranges keep related rows together but create hot spots, hashing spreads load, consistent hashing eases resharding, and a lookup table adds flexibility and a hop.

content.statement: With at-least-once delivery, a consumer never receives the same message twice.

remember: At-least-once means a message can arrive more than once, so consumers must handle duplicates.

content.prompt: Signup sends a welcome email through a slow mail API. Why put the email on a queue instead of calling the API during the request?

options.text: Signup returns at once, and the email can be retried if the mail API is down
The email reaches the user sooner than with a direct call
A queue guarantees the email is never sent twice
The queue makes the mail API itself respond faster

remember: A queue lets the request finish now and the slow or flaky work happen later, with retries.

content.prompt: If the worker crashes in the middle of charge_card, that order is never charged, although the broker redelivers unacknowledged messages. Find the bug.
content.code:
def on_message(msg):
    order = json.loads(msg.body)
    msg.ack()
    charge_card(order)
    send_receipt(order)

fixes.text: Wrap charge_card in try/except and log the error
Move msg.ack() above json.loads
Move msg.ack() below send_receipt(order)

remember: Acknowledge a message only after the work is done; acking first turns a crash into a lost message.

content.prompt: An order service must save each order and publish an OrderCreated event, losing neither if it crashes. Put the transactional outbox steps in order.

steps.text: A relay process reads unsent rows from the outbox table
Commit the transaction
Mark the outbox row as sent
Insert the order and the event row in one transaction
Publish the event to the message broker

remember: Save the event in the same transaction as the data, publish it, and only then mark it sent; a crash causes a resend, never a loss.

content.prompt: The broker delivers each message at least once. tx is the open transaction; a call on db commits on its own at once. Fill the blank so each payment is applied exactly once.

options.text: msg.ack()
cache.set(key, True)
db.insert("processed", key)
tx.insert("processed", key)

remember: Record a message as processed in the same transaction as its effect, so both happen or neither does.

content.statement: During a network partition, a system can answer on every node and still guarantee that each read sees the latest write.

remember: CAP: when the network splits, a system must either refuse some requests (consistency) or risk stale answers (availability).

content.prompt: A network partition cuts a database cluster in two. The smaller side refuses writes until the network heals. What did the system choose?

options.text: Availability over consistency
Consistency over availability
Low latency over durability
Neither: it gave up partition tolerance

remember: Refusing requests to avoid conflicting data during a partition is choosing consistency (CP); answering anyway is choosing availability (AP).

content.prompt: A leaderless store keeps n copies of each key. A write waits for w replicas, a read asks r replicas. Fill the blank so every read reaches at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write.
content.code:
def read_sees_latest_write(n, w, r):
    return w + r ____ n

remember: Read and write quorums are sure to overlap only when w + r > n; with n = 3, w = 2 and r = 2 every read meets the latest write.

content.prompt: Two replicas accepted writes during a partition. On merge, the higher timestamp wins. Node A's clock runs 5 seconds fast. What does this print?

options.text: 2 items
1 item

remember: Last-write-wins trusts clocks; with clock skew it silently drops the write that really happened later.

content.prompt: CAP only covers what happens during a network partition. With no partition, what must a geo-replicated database still trade off on each request?

options.text: Latency against consistency: waiting for distant replicas makes requests slower
Availability against partition tolerance
Durability against the size of the data set
Consistency against partition tolerance

remember: PACELC: during a partition choose availability or consistency; otherwise choose between low latency and consistency.

content.statement: An uptime of 99.9 % still allows almost nine hours of downtime a year.

remember: Each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold: 99.9 % is about 8.8 hours a year, 99.99 % under an hour.

content.prompt: Two app servers sit behind one load balancer and share one database. Which change removes a single point of failure?

options.text: Give the database server twice the RAM
Add a third app server
Add a standby database that takes over if the first one fails
Log every request in more detail

remember: A single point of failure is any one part whose loss stops the system; remove it with a redundant copy that can take over.

content.prompt: An SLA promises uptime per 30-day month. What does this print?
content.code:
minutes_per_month = 30 * 24 * 60
allowed = [round(minutes_per_month * (100 - sla) / 100, 1)
           for sla in (99.95, 99.99)]
print(allowed)

remember: Allowed downtime is the period times (1 - availability): 99.95 % of a month is about 22 minutes, 99.99 % about 4.

content.prompt: When the payment API is slow, some customers are charged two or three times for one order. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Create one key per order, such as f"order-{order_id}", before the loop
Raise the timeout to 30 seconds
Sleep a fixed 1 second instead of 2 ** attempt

remember: A retry must reuse the same idempotency key; a new key per attempt makes every retry look like a new payment.

content.prompt: Match each resilience pattern with what it does.

right.text: Gives each dependency its own small pool of threads or connections
Stops waiting for a slow call after a set time
After many failures, fails calls at once for a while without trying
Repeats a failed call after growing, randomized pauses

remember: Timeouts bound waiting, jittered retries ride out blips, circuit breakers stop hammering a failing service, and bulkheads keep one slow dependency from starving the rest.

content.statement: Splitting a monolith into microservices turns in-process function calls into network calls that can time out or fail.

remember: Every service boundary is a network call: slower, and able to fail in ways a function call cannot.

content.prompt: What is the main benefit teams expect from splitting a large monolith into microservices?

options.text: Each call between parts of the system gets faster
Debugging gets easier because there is less code in one place
Teams can deploy and scale their parts independently
The system needs fewer servers in total

remember: Microservices buy independent deploys and scaling per team, paid for with network calls and operational complexity.

content.prompt: The orders and billing services read and write each other's tables in one shared database. What is the biggest problem with this?

options.text: The database cannot serve two services' connections at once
A schema change for one service can break the other, so they cannot be deployed independently
Reads between the two services become eventually consistent
Both services must be written in the same programming language

remember: Services that share tables are coupled through the schema; give each service its own data and talk through APIs or events.

content.prompt: You move billing out of a monolith step by step (the strangler fig approach). Put the steps in order.

steps.text: Send all billing traffic to the new service
Delete the billing code from the monolith
Build the billing service next to the monolith
Send a small share of billing traffic to the new service

remember: Strangle a monolith gradually: build alongside it, shift a little traffic, then all of it, and delete the old code last.

content.prompt: Three of these keep data in step across microservices without one transaction spanning several services' databases. Which is the odd one out?

items.text: A saga with compensating steps
A transactional outbox that publishes events
Two-phase commit across the services' databases
Services updating their own copies from published events

remember: Microservices usually avoid two-phase commit and use sagas, outboxes and events instead, accepting eventual consistency.
